title: The Great Nuclear Winter Debate of 1983
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss nuclear winter, the theory that smoke from fires after a large-scale nuclear war would block sunlight and cool the planet. They cover the Cold War context, the Reagan-era Star Wars (SDI) debate, volcanic precedents (Krakatoa 1883, Mount Tambora 1815 and the Year Without a Summer), Carl Sagan and Richard Turco's scenarios and the TTAPS paper, the later "nuclear autumn" revision, critiques by nuclear proliferation hawks and Michael Crichton, the Doomsday Clock moving to three minutes to midnight, and Sagan's proposed arms reduction. The episode ends with listener mail thanks.

entities.name: Atomic Scientists Science and Security Board

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to nuclear winter
segments.summary: Hosts joke around, then introduce the topic of nuclear winter, its aftereffects rather than immediate blast damage, and the controversy it sparked in the 1980s.

segments.title: Origins of the debate and the Star Wars context
segments.summary: Hawkish scientists challenged nuclear winter science in academic journals, tied to the debate over Reagan's SDI missile defense program and nuclear arms race, with arguments about scientific certainty.

segments.title: Atmospheric balance, smoke, and volcanic precedents
segments.summary: The sun's delicate balance with Earth is described. Nuclear winter would come mainly from smoke from fires. Past volcanic eruptions are cited: Krakatoa in 1883 and Mount Tambora in 1815, which caused the Year Without a Summer.

segments.title: Sagan's oil fire prediction and misplaced arguments
segments.summary: Sagan's prediction about the burning oil fields in the early 1990s did not pan out as badly as predicted. The hosts discuss how that does not justify building more nuclear weapons.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Break between segments with a short banter about a Facebook post and science wording.

segments.title: KT boundary extinction and impact winter
segments.summary: Hosts mention the impact winter theory that the asteroid strike at the Cretaceous-Tertiary boundary may have killed the dinosaurs, comparing it to nuclear winter.

segments.title: Nuclear winter scenarios by size of war
segments.summary: Sagan and Turco's scenarios range from minimal to extreme, from a small attack to full-scale war with thousands of warheads. Effects include reduced sunlight, temperature drops, and ozone loss, with the Southern Hemisphere least affected in the smaller scenarios. Hosts discuss the scenarios and the Hiroshima black rain.

segments.title: Publicizing the TTAPS paper and the nuclear autumn revision
segments.summary: Sagan and colleagues published the TTAPS paper in Science, and Sagan wrote articles in Parade and Foreign Affairs, drawing criticism that this was fearmongering. Seven years later the report was revised as Nuclear Autumn, with less dire numbers. Uncertainties about smoke amounts, atmospheric persistence, and season are discussed.

segments.title: Ocean ecosystems, critics, and science by consensus
segments.summary: Ozone loss could expose phytoplankton to damaging UV, threatening the marine food chain. Conservative critics, including Michael Crichton, attacked nuclear winter as science by consensus and politicized science. Newer climate models suggest the effects might be worse, and a regional war scenario is discussed.

segments.title: Doomsday Clock and arms reduction
segments.summary: The Doomsday Clock was moved to three minutes to midnight in January, with reasons including nuclear modernization and climate change. Sagan proposed reducing arsenals to a threshold below which nuclear winter would not occur, which no one adopted.

segments.title: Listener mail and thank-yous
segments.summary: Hosts read thank-you notes for gifts from listeners, including homemade nougat, chocolate, cheese, books, and currency notes.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give social media and website contact info and sign off.
